title: Post-Crash Diagnosis: What Broke & Why
html:
First rule: power down, then think

A crash dumps kinetic energy into the cheapest thing that will yield: props first, then arms, then shafts, then wires. Before you touch anything, disconnect the LiPo. A crash can short ESC pads, pinch a motor wire against carbon, or crack a capacitor lead. Re-powering a shorted quad turns a $4 motor repair into a fried flight controller and, occasionally, a fire. Sniff the quad: hot electronics and vented LiPo both have a distinct sweet, sharp smell.

SAFETY.
Disconnect the battery and remove props before any inspection. Inspect the LiPo separately for impact damage or puffing before you ever charge it again (see 11.6).

The systematic walk-around

Diagnose in the same order every time so nothing gets missed. Energy travels from the point of impact inward, so follow it.

  1. Props. Run a fingernail around each blade. Chips, nicks, and hairline cracks cause vibration that the gyro reads as noise. A blade that looks fine can be cracked at the hub. When in doubt, bin it.
  2. Motors. Spin each bell by hand. A grinding or gritty feel means dirt or a damaged bearing; a notchy catch means a bent shaft. Wiggle the bell axially and radially. Bent shafts show as a visible wobble when you spin the bell against a fixed point.
  3. Arms. Flex each arm gently. Carbon fails by delamination, not bending. Look for white stress lines, a fuzzy frayed edge, or a soft spongy feel. A cracked arm flies once more and then snaps mid-throttle.
  4. Wiring. Tug each motor wire near the solder joint. Crashes pull wires; the copper can fracture inside intact insulation. Check the XT60/XT30 leads and the capacitor.
  5. Stack and FC. Look for cracked solder joints, lifted pads, a snapped barometer, or a camera/VTX antenna torn loose.

Reading the gyro: what likely broke and why

Symptom on next armLikely causeWhy
One motor stutters / hotBent shaft or dragging bellIncreased mechanical load; ESC fights it
Tilts hard on takeoffReversed or dead motor, swapped after repairWrong rotation or no thrust on one corner
Violent oscillationCracked prop or loose motor screwVibration the filters can't reject
No videoTorn VTX antenna / cracked u.FLAntenna takes the impact on flips
Won't arm at allShorted ESC, snapped gyro, lost RXDirect impact to the stack
Insight.
A bent shaft is the single most common hidden crash injury on 5-inch quads. Always spin every bell by hand before you celebrate that "it survived."
crash-triage checklist
# power OFF, props OFF, then: 1. smell test ............ no hot/sweet odor 2. 4x props .............. nick/crack -> replace 3. 4x bells by hand ...... grind/wobble = shaft 4. 4x arms flex .......... white lines = delam 5. tug motor wires ....... broken strands 6. stack visual .......... lifted pads, caps 7. antennas .............. VTX + RX intact
▸Hands-On

Produce a prioritized damage report for a crashed quad (or photos of one).

  1. Power off, remove props, and run the 7-step triage above.
  2. List every issue you find with a likely cause for each.
  3. Rank them: flight-blocking (cracked arm, bent shaft) vs cosmetic (scuffed canopy).
  4. Decide go / no-go and the order of repairs before next power-up.

title: Soldering Repairs: Motors, Props, Arms & Antennas
html:
The right iron and the right heat

Most failed FPV repairs are cold joints from an underpowered iron. Use a temperature-controlled iron of at least 60W (a TS100/TS101 or Pinecil at 80W is the hobby standard) with a chisel/bevel tip, not a pencil tip. Set ~350-370 C for general work and bump to 380-400 C for thick battery pads and ground planes that sink heat. Use leaded 63/37 rosin-core solder if legal where you are; it flows easier and is far more forgiving than lead-free for beginners. A tub of no-clean flux is the secret to clean joints.

Insight.
A good joint is shiny and concave, wetting both surfaces. A dull, blobby, or ball-shaped joint is cold. Re-flow it with flux, don't pile on more solder.

Technique that always works

  1. Tin both sides first. Pre-tin the pad and the wire end separately. Then bring them together and heat until the two pools merge.
  2. Heat the joint, feed solder to the joint - never melt solder on the iron and wipe it on.
  3. 3-second rule. If a joint isn't flowing in ~3 seconds, your iron is too cold or too small. Stop before you cook the pad off the board (a lifted pad is a real repair, not a cosmetic one).
  4. Keep the tip tinned and wipe it on brass wool between joints.

Replacing a motor

Note the wire order before you desolder (photograph it). Motor wire order does not set direction on bidirectional DShot/BLHeli_S/AM32 ESCs - you fix rotation in software - but keeping it tidy avoids confusion. Desolder the three pads, route the new motor's wires the same way, trim to length, tin, and solder. Then set rotation in Betaflight's Motors tab or via your ESC's motor-direction option. Spin-test at low throttle props off and confirm direction with a slip of paper or by watching the bell.

SAFETY.
Props OFF for every bench spin-up. Before power-up after any solder work, inspect for solder bridges between adjacent pads and beep out battery + and - with a multimeter in continuity mode. A bridge across the battery pads is an instant dead short.

Arms, props, and antennas

  • Arms: on a unibody frame, replace the whole bottom plate; on a replaceable-arm frame, swap just the arm. Torque arm bolts to snug, then add a dab of medium (blue) threadlocker on the nut, not the carbon.
  • Props: match size, pitch, and rotation exactly; balance isn't worth chasing on modern quads, but matched sets are. Torque prop nuts firmly - a thrown prop in flight is a missile.
  • Antennas: VTX antennas die most. If the u.FL/IPEX connector survived, just clip on a new antenna. If the pigtail tore off the board, resolder the u.FL or fit an MMCX-pigtail VTX next time - far more crash-durable. Never power a VTX without an antenna: you can cook the PA.
motor swap - direction set (CLI)
# after resolder, props OFF, on bench: set motor_pwm_protocol = DSHOT600 save # Betaflight Motors tab: enable, spin one # wrong way? toggle direction: Configure ESC -> Motor Direction Reversed # confirm all 4 spin inward-top per layout
▸Hands-On

Replace one motor (or practice a full desolder/resolder on a bench motor).

  1. Photograph wire routing, then desolder the three motor pads.
  2. Tin pads and new wires separately; reflow to join. Aim for shiny concave joints.
  3. Multimeter-check for bridges; beep out battery +/-.
  4. Bench-spin props OFF, set correct rotation in software, confirm a clean joint.

title: Diagnosing Common Faults: No Video & Won't Arm
html:
Diagnose like a binary search

Every fault has a chain from input to output. Don't guess - test the midpoint, decide which half is broken, and split again. This finds root cause in minutes instead of replacing parts at random.

No video

The chain is: camera -> VTX -> antenna -> air -> goggle antenna -> goggle RX. Work it end to end.

  1. Confirm the VTX is powered and not in pit mode. Many VTXs boot in 0 mW pit mode. Check the LED and the OSD. A VTX with no antenna may have damaged its PA - this is why "no video" sometimes follows a crash that tore the antenna.
  2. Channel/band match. Goggles and VTX must share band and channel (e.g. Raceband R1 = 5658 MHz). One digit off = static.
  3. Analog vs digital. On digital (DJI/HDZero/Walksnail) a no-video is usually a loose camera coax, an unbound/unpaired air unit, or overheating shutdown - feel if the air unit is scalding.
  4. Camera vs VTX. Blue/black screen with a clean OSD = camera dead or unplugged; OSD also gone = VTX or its feed. Swap the camera or VTX to isolate.
  5. Antenna. Cracked u.FL or a snapped element drops range to a few feet. Wiggle-test while watching for breakup.
SAFETY.
Never bench-test a VTX without its antenna fitted. Running a VTX antenna-less reflects RF power back into the amplifier and can permanently kill it.

Won't arm

Betaflight refuses to arm and tells you why. Read the arming flags in the OSD ("arming disabled" with a reason) or type status in the CLI. Decode the flag instead of guessing.

Arming flagMeaningFix
NOGYROGyro not detectedCracked gyro / loose stack solder; reflash, reseat, replace FC
RXLOSSNo valid RC linkBind RX, check UART/protocol, power the TX
THROTTLEThrottle not at minLower stick; recalibrate endpoints
ANGLE / CRASHQuad not level / crash-recovery latchPlace flat; re-level the quad
BOXFAILSAFEFailsafe switch activeClear the assigned switch
CALIBSensors calibratingHold still on power-up
ARMSWITCHArm switch was on at bootToggle arm off then on
Insight.
90% of "won't arm" reports are RXLOSS (link/protocol mismatch), throttle not at minimum, or the arm switch being on at boot. Check those three before suspecting hardware.
betaflight CLI - status
# status MCU ... GYRO detected Arming disable flags: RXLOSS THROTTLE # two reasons - fix both: RXLOSS -> rx link down, rebind / check serialrx_provider THROTTLE -> throttle channel above min, recalibrate
▸Hands-On

Work a no-video and a won't-arm fault tree to resolution.

  1. Induce or imagine each fault on your build (or a written scenario).
  2. For no-video, walk camera->VTX->antenna->goggle and note where signal is lost.
  3. For won't-arm, read the arming flags via OSD or status and decode each.
  4. Document every step and the confirmed root cause and fix.

title: Diagnosing Motor Desync & Oscillations
html:
Three failures that feel similar in the air

Desync, oscillation, and mechanical noise all show as the quad misbehaving, but they have different fingerprints. Learn to tell them apart from the symptom and you skip hours of random tuning.

Motor desync

Desync is the ESC losing track of where the rotor is, so it stops commutating - the motor cuts out, sometimes with a distinct brrrap grind, then catches again or the quad flips. It typically happens on fast throttle changes: hard punch-outs or sudden chops, especially low-RPM-to-high transitions.

  • Causes: ESC firmware/timing mismatch, motor too low-Kv-for-protocol edge cases, demag/timing set wrong, a damaged ESC FET, or motor bell rubbing.
  • Fixes: on BLHeli_S/AM32/Bluejay set timing to medium-high or high and try a higher PWM frequency (e.g. 48 kHz on Bluejay), enable/keep bidirectional DShot and RPM filtering, update ESC firmware, and lower motor_output_limit while you test. Confirm the bell spins freely first.

Oscillations

Oscillation is the control loop fighting itself: a buzz, a hot motor, or visible shaking. Two flavors:

  • High-frequency hot motors / coil whine: too much D-gain or insufficient filtering. Motors get hot on a hover with no aggressive flying. Lower D, check gyro/D-term filtering, ensure RPM filter is working.
  • Low-frequency wobble (slow bounce): too much P relative to D, or a propwash-handling problem. Tune the PD ratio; modern Betaflight presets help.
Insight.
Hot motors after a gentle flight = oscillation/filtering, not a weak motor. Touch each motor right after landing: anything too hot to hold comfortably (well above ~50 C) is being driven by oscillation.

Mechanical noise vs the rest

The gyro can't tell vibration from real movement. A cracked prop, a loose motor screw, a bent shaft, or a soft mount feeds garbage into the loop, which the PID then amplifies. Before touching the tune, eliminate mechanical sources. Use the Betaflight Blackbox + spectrum/PSD viewer: a sharp peak that tracks motor RPM is mechanical; broadband noise points at filtering/tune.

SymptomMost likelyFirst fix
Cutout / flip on punch-outDesyncESC timing high, update FW, bidir DShot
Hot motors on a calm hoverHF oscillationLower D, verify filters/RPM filter
Slow bounce in turnsLF oscillationAdjust P:D ratio
One corner vibrates / RPM-tracking peakMechanicalReplace prop, tighten/replace motor, check shaft
SAFETY.
Always diagnose with props removed unless you are deliberately doing a tethered/secured throttle test. A desync that flips a quad on the bench with props on can lacerate you.
anti-desync ESC settings (Bluejay)
Motor Timing ......... 22-24 (med-high) PWM Frequency ........ 48 kHz Demag Compensation ... High Bidirectional DShot .. ON (RPM filter) Betaflight: motor_output_limit = 80 while testing
▸Hands-On

Match described symptoms to desync vs oscillation vs mechanical and propose a fix.

  1. Take 3-4 symptoms (recorded clips, Blackbox logs, or written descriptions).
  2. Classify each using the table above.
  3. For mechanical, name the part to replace; for tune/ESC, name the exact setting to change.
  4. If you have a quad, verify one fix props-off and re-test.

title: LiPo Care: Charging, Storage Voltage & Balancing
html:
The voltage map of a cell

Every LiPo decision comes back to per-cell voltage. Memorize these and you'll double pack lifespan.

StateVolts/cell6S pack
Full charge4.20 V25.2 V
Storage3.80-3.85 V~22.9 V
Land by3.5 V resting21.0 V
Damage zonebelow 3.0 Vbelow 18.0 V

Charging correctly

Charge in balance mode through the balance lead, not just the main lead. The charger then equalizes all cells to within a few millivolts. Default charge rate is 1C (a 1300mAh pack = 1.3A); modern high-C race packs tolerate 2-3C but every charge above 1C costs cycle life and adds heat. Set the charger's cell count manually and confirm it matches the pack before starting - a wrong cell count is a classic fire cause.

SAFETY.
Never charge unattended. Charge inside a fire-safe LiPo bag or ammo can, on a non-flammable surface, away from anything that burns. Never charge a pack that is warm from flight, puffed, or physically damaged. Let packs cool to room temperature first.

Storage voltage - the single biggest longevity lever

A LiPo left at 4.2V degrades fast; left flat below 3.0V it may be permanently damaged. Store at 3.80-3.85V/cell. If a pack won't fly within ~2-3 days, storage-charge (or storage-discharge) it. Most chargers have a one-button STORAGE mode that charges or bleeds the pack to ~3.8V/cell automatically. A pack stored properly at room temperature loses very little capacity over months.

Reading pack health from the balance numbers

After a flight, check the per-cell voltages on the charger or a cell checker. A healthy pack lands with cells within ~0.03V of each other. Watch for:

  • Drift: one cell consistently 0.05-0.1V lower than the rest = that cell is aging or damaged. The pack will sag and trip your low-voltage cutoff early.
  • Hard sag: voltage that recovers a lot after landing (e.g. lands at 3.4V, rests at 3.8V) means high internal resistance - an old or tired pack.
  • IR readings: chargers like the ISDT/iCharger show per-cell internal resistance. A cell reading much higher mOhm than its siblings is failing; retire the pack.
Insight.
Treat storage voltage like flossing: boring, easy to skip, and the thing that actually determines whether your $30 pack lasts 50 cycles or 300. Storage-charge the moment a flying session ends if you won't fly again soon.
charger - storage charge a 6S pack
Program: LiPo STORAGE Cells: 6S (confirm = pack label) Current: 1.0C Target: 3.80 V/cell start -> charges/bleeds to ~22.9V cells: 3.81 3.80 3.81 3.80 3.82 3.80 balanced cells: 3.81 3.80 3.72 3.80 3.81 3.80 cell 3 drifting
▸Hands-On

Storage-charge a LiPo and log its balance.

  1. Confirm cell count, set charger to STORAGE at 1C, balance lead connected, in a fire-safe bag.
  2. Run to ~3.80V/cell.
  3. Record each cell's voltage (and IR if available).
  4. Flag any cell drifting more than ~0.05V and note it for retirement watch.

title: LiPo Safety: Swelling, Fire & Safe Disposal
html:
What swelling means

A puffed or swollen LiPo has generated internal gas from electrolyte breakdown - the chemistry has begun to fail and the cell is unstable. A pack that has even slight rounding of its flat faces is on a one-way trip. A swollen pack is retired immediately. It will not get better, it will get worse, and a stressed cell can go into thermal runaway and ignite without warning.

SAFETY.
Causes of a fire: over-charge, over-discharge below 3.0V/cell, physical/puncture damage, charging a warm pack, wrong cell-count on the charger, and internal shorts from crash impact. A LiPo fire is self-sustaining (the pack carries its own oxidizer) - you cannot smother it like a normal fire.

Inspecting your fleet

  • Puffing: lay each pack on a flat surface; it should sit flat and rock-free. Any bulge = retire.
  • Casing: torn shrink wrap, dented cells, or exposed foil = retire.
  • Leads/connectors: frayed wire, scorched XT60, wobbly balance plug = repair or retire.
  • Behavior: abnormal heat after charge/flight, fast self-discharge, or a cell that won't balance = retire.

Fire-safe storage and handling

Store packs at 3.8V/cell, at room temperature, in a non-flammable container kept away from living space and exits. Good options, in rough order of protection: a metal ammo can (lid cracked, not sealed, so pressure can vent), a steel cabinet, or a dedicated fireproof LiPo safe. Avoid stacking heavy items on packs. Keep a Class D-rated extinguisher or a large bucket of dry sand nearby; in practice, the realistic plan for a small pack fire is to move it (with tongs, if safe) onto a non-flammable surface outdoors and let it burn out, while protecting yourself from the toxic smoke.

Discharge and disposal

Before disposal a pack must be fully discharged. Two accepted methods:

  1. Charger discharge: use the charger's discharge function to bring cells down to ~0V where supported.
  2. Salt-water bath: submerge the pack in a bucket of heavily salted water for several days (this is the classic hobby method to drain residual charge through the leads). Do this outdoors in a non-metallic bucket, expect gassing, then check the leads read ~0V before handling.

Once discharged, do not put LiPos in household trash or regular recycling. Take them to a battery-recycling drop-off: Call2Recycle locations, many hobby shops, big-box electronics retailers, and household hazardous-waste facilities accept them. Tape over the terminals before transport.

Rule.
Disposal and transport rules vary by location, and air-travel rules (carry-on only, terminal protection, watt-hour limits) are set by your airline and aviation authority. Verify current local hazardous-waste and your carrier's battery rules before transporting or shipping packs.
Insight.
Label retired packs the moment you condemn them ("DEAD - DISCARD") and physically separate them from your flight bag. Most LiPo fires come from a packed-with-good-ones reject that someone charged by mistake.
▸Hands-On

Audit your fleet and build a fire-safe storage solution.

  1. Lay every pack flat; flag any puffing, casing, or lead damage; retire and label the rejects.
  2. Set up a non-flammable storage container (ammo can / LiPo safe) for the keepers at 3.8V/cell.
  3. Salt-water or charger-discharge one retired pack to ~0V.
  4. Find and write down a local battery recycling/drop-off option.

title: Firmware Updates, Upkeep & Sensible Upgrades
html:
Update on purpose, not on impulse

A firmware update can fix a real bug or wipe a tune you spent a season dialing in. Update when there's a reason: a security/safety fix, a feature you need, or new hardware support - not just because a new version exists. The week before a big event is the worst time to flash.

The safe update routine

  1. Back up everything first. In the Betaflight CLI type diff all (or dump all) and save the output to a text file. This is your full config and your insurance policy.
  2. Read the changelog and migration notes. Major versions (e.g. 4.4 -> 4.5) can rename or drop settings, so a blind paste of an old diff won't fully restore.
  3. Flash with "Full chip erase" on a major upgrade to avoid leftover corrupt settings; keep target and build options matched to your board.
  4. Restore selectively. Re-apply your rates, filters, and tune by hand or via a reviewed diff, watching for warnings about unknown commands.
  5. Re-verify the safety-critical items every time (next section).
SAFETY.
After any firmware update, re-verify failsafe and flight modes before flying. Stick endpoints, arm switch, motor directions, and especially failsafe stage 2 (drop/land) can reset to defaults. Do a props-off bench test, then a confirmed failsafe test (power off the TX and watch the motors stop), then a low hover.

Routine upkeep beyond firmware

  • Keep your radio/ELRS TX and RX on matching firmware - a version mismatch can break binding.
  • Re-calibrate the accelerometer after a hard crash or board reflash.
  • Periodically re-flash ESC firmware (Bluejay/AM32) when desync or efficiency fixes land.
  • Keep a per-quad config folder with the latest diff all so any board swap is a 2-minute restore.

Sensible upgrades

Spend where it changes outcomes, not where it looks cool. Good value upgrades:

UpgradeBenefitWorth it when
ELRS RX (from older protocol)Range, latency, link reliabilityRange failsafes or twitchy link
Digital FPV / better VTX antennaClearer feed, fewer crashes from breakupAnalog static is causing crashes
Higher-quality propsLess vibration, cleaner tuneHot motors / noisy gyro traces
GPS module + rescueReturn-to-home safety netFlying long range / over LOS edge
Better LiPos / more packsMore flight time per sessionOld packs sag early
Insight.
The highest-ROI "upgrade" is usually fresh props and a healthy battery, not a new flight controller. Fix the thing that's actually limiting you.
betaflight CLI - backup before flashing
# diff all # ...copy ALL output to quadname_4.5_backup.txt... # now flash; after reboot, re-verify: # get failsafe # status (check arming flags, modes) # TX off -> motors must stop (failsafe test)
▸Hands-On

Back up your config and document a safe update routine.

  1. Run diff all and save the output to a dated, named file.
  2. Write your step-by-step update routine, including the post-update failsafe and modes re-check.
  3. Pick one justified upgrade for your setup and write the expected benefit and the trigger that makes it worth it.

title: The Pre/Post-Flight Maintenance Checklist
html:
Why a checklist beats experience

Even experienced pilots crash from things a 60-second check would have caught: a loose prop nut, a cracked arm from yesterday, a battery strap fraying. A written, repeatable checklist removes "I think I checked that" from the equation. Pilots and aviation use checklists for exactly this reason - the goal is to make the right check happen every single time, not just when you remember.

Pre-flight (every flight)

  1. Props: correct rotation per corner, no nicks/cracks, nuts tight. A thrown prop is the #1 injury cause - check this first.
  2. Frame & arms: flex each arm, check for white stress lines; verify standoffs and stack screws are snug.
  3. Motors: spin each by hand - smooth, no grind; motor screws not backed out (they hit the windings if too long/loose).
  4. Battery: not puffed, fully charged, strap good and tight; lead and connector intact.
  5. Antennas: VTX and RX antennas present and undamaged. Never power a VTX antenna-less.
  6. Link & modes: RX bound, arm switch off, modes correct, failsafe configured.
  7. Surroundings: people, airspace, and a clear arm/launch area.
SAFETY.
Prop, frame, and battery checks happen on every flight without exception. Arm only when the quad is pointed away from people and you have called it clear. Disarm before anyone approaches the quad.

Post-flight (every flight)

  1. Battery voltage: read resting per-cell. Landed below 3.5V/cell? You're flying too long - shorten the timer.
  2. Motor temps: touch each motor. Too hot to hold = oscillation/filtering issue to fix before next session (see 11.4).
  3. Damage scan: any contact/crash this session? Re-run the post-crash triage from 11.1.
  4. Storage charge: if done flying for a while, storage-charge packs to 3.8V/cell.
  5. Log it: note anything off so it gets fixed at the bench, not rediscovered in the air.
Insight.
The post-flight battery and motor-temp check is your early-warning system. A pack that lands hot or a motor that runs hot is telling you about a failure before it becomes a crash.
WhenCatches
Pre-flight props/nutsThrown prop, desync from loose screw
Pre-flight arm flexCracked carbon snapping mid-flight
Pre-flight failsafe/modesFlyaway, arming surprises
Post-flight cell voltageOver-discharge damage, tired packs
Post-flight motor tempOscillation / filtering problems early
pocket checklist (laminate this)
PRE: props ok+tight | arms ok | motors spin | batt ok+strapped | antennas on | bound/modes/failsafe | area clear ARM only pointed away, called clear POST: cell V >=3.5 | motors cool | damage scan | storage-charge | log issues
▸Hands-On

Build, laminate, and run your own pre/post-flight checklist.

  1. Write your pre-flight and post-flight items, tailored to your quad and field.
  2. Print and laminate it (or put it in your phone) so it travels in the flight bag.
  3. Run it through one full flight cycle.
  4. Log anything it caught and refine the list.
